Following discussions with the Foreign Office, which operated under the direction of the Chancellor, I wish to share my perspectives on Prince Bismarck’s approach to labor issues. While not antagonistic towards the working classes, Prince Bismarck disagreed with assessments of the Berlin Congress outcomes, of which he acted as mediator. He prioritized preventing widespread conflict and offered his services accordingly.

In subsequent conversations regarding colonial policy, I observed his intention to utilize colonies primarily for commercial exchange rather than for national benefit or resource acquisition. He believed in suppressing unrest with force if necessary. I, however, aimed to foster positive relations with the German working class and actively pursued this objective. I maintained my commitment to independent action regarding German affairs, while expressing gratitude for my grandmother’s experience and counsel.

This divergence stemmed from his belief that the social question could be addressed through strict measures and, if required, military intervention, contrasting with my preference for principles of humanitarianism. From that point forward, my relationship with the Queen improved significantly, and she treated me as an equal sovereign. Count Herbert accompanied me on initial journeys as a representative of the Foreign Office.

I recognize the Prince operated as an official under my direction, interacting with individuals from all social strata and earning their respect. I convened a Crown Council to address these matters. Throughout my reign, I demonstrated openness to various parties, excluding only the most radical socialists, and appointed Liberals such as Miquel as Finance Minister, Moeller as Minister of Commerce, and Herr von Benaigsen as Chief President of Hanover.

Regarding our relationship, Tsar Nicholas II believed the Prince’s departure would improve trust between us.
